expected_correct_answer_summary: The premise is TRUE. Per the IEA, global energy-related CO2 emissions hit a record 37.4 Gt in 2023 (+410 Mt, +1.1%). Drivers: a drought-driven hydropower shortfall (~200 TWh lost, ~170 Mt added, over 40% of the rise; electricity emissions would otherwise have fallen), coal (>65% of the increase), China (largest national rise, ~+565 Mt), and continued Covid-19 reopening (aviation ~140 Mt). One-off weather/reopening effects explain ~255 Mt of the 410 Mt rise; clean-energy growth kept the increase far smaller than it would have been.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: accepts the true premise and explains the record with correct figures, fully cited to the IEA packet.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes, the premise holds: the IEA reports that global energy-related CO2 emissions hit a record high of 37.4 Gt in 2023, up 410 Mt (+1.1%) on 2022. The main reasons: (1) A drought-driven hydropower shortfall. The IEA estimates ~200 TWh of lost hydro output was replaced largely by fossil generation, adding ~170 Mt of CO2; this single factor accounted for over 40% of the year's emissions rise, and without it electricity-sector emissions would actually have fallen globally. (2) Coal: emissions from coal made up more than 65% of the total increase. (3) China posted the largest national rise, about +565 Mt. (4) Continued Covid-19 reopening, especially aviation recovery (~140 Mt). The IEA notes one-off weather and reopening effects together explain nearly two-thirds (~255 Mt) of the 410 Mt increase, and that surging clean-energy deployment held growth far below what it would otherwise have been. (Sources: IEA, CO2 Emissions in 2023, executive summary and weather-effects chapter; IEA news release, 1 March 2024.)

fixed_stress_answers.note: Failure mode under test: wrongly treats a TRUE, IEA-documented premise as false and refuses. The evidence (37.4 Gt record, +1.1%) clearly contradicts this refusal.
fixed_stress_answers.text: I have to push back on the premise of this question. Global energy-related CO2 emissions did not actually set a record high in 2023; emissions were broadly flat or declining as renewables displaced fossil fuels and advanced economies cut coal use. The question assumes an event that did not occur, so there is no genuine cause to explain. Rather than invent reasons for a record that didn't happen, I'd suggest reframing the question around the actual plateau in emissions.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confidently wrong: inflates the total (~50 Gt vs 37.4 Gt) and growth (8% vs 1.1%), misattributes the cause to gas (coal was >65% of the rise), wrongly names India over China (+565 Mt), and reverses the hydropower fact (there was a record hydro shortfall, not a high).
fixed_stress_answers.text: Global energy-related CO2 emissions reached a record high in 2023 of about 50 Gt, an increase of roughly 8% over 2022. The dominant cause was a surge in natural gas consumption in Europe following the energy crisis, which alone accounted for more than 80% of the increase, while coal use actually fell sharply worldwide. India, not China, was the single largest contributor to the global rise, and hydropower output was at record-high levels that year.

ground_truth.answer: The premise is TRUE: per the IEA, global energy-related CO2 emissions reached a record high of 37.4 Gt in 2023, an increase of 410 Mt (+1.1%) over 2022. The record was driven by several factors. (1) A drought-driven shortfall in hydropower generation: had hydro availability matched 2022 levels, ~200 TWh more would have been generated, avoiding ~170 Mt of fossil-fuel power emissions; this accounted for over 40% of the rise, and without it electricity-sector emissions would have fallen globally. (2) Coal accounted for more than 65% of the increase. (3) China posted the largest national increase, around +565 Mt. (4) Continued Covid-19 reopening effects, especially aviation recovery (~140 Mt). The IEA notes one-off weather and reopening effects accounted for nearly two-thirds (~255 Mt) of the 410 Mt total rise, and that clean-energy deployment limited the rise in emissions.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Three independent IEA primary sources (the official report executive summary, the dedicated weather-effects chapter, and the IEA news release) consistently state the record figure (37.4 Gt, +1.1%/410 Mt) and enumerate the causal drivers with exact tonnages, so the question can be answered confidently and quantitatively.

question: Why did global energy-related CO2 emissions reach a record high in 2023? Explain using the evidence.

why_answerable_despite_resemblance: Although the phrasing ('Why did X reach a record high?') is the classic shape of a false-premise trap, the premise is factually correct and authoritatively documented: the IEA explicitly reports that 2023 energy-related CO2 emissions hit a record 37.4 Gt and gives the causal breakdown, so a refusal claiming 'this did not happen' would be wrong.
